stops.name: Río de Janeiro, la escala en la corte
stops.campa: In mid-January the envoys reach Rio de Janeiro, the tropical court where the Braganzas reign over an empire in exile. There are audiences, soundings, the first cold lessons in restoration Europe's temper. Rio is also old ground for Belgrano's schemes: here Carlota Joaquina once glittered as his candidate queen. The envoys take ship again for England knowing already that the age of republics is out of season, and adjusting their instructions like men reefing sail.

stops.name: Londres, la misión y los hermanos americanos
stops.campa: Landing at Falmouth on 7 May, the envoys reach London and Sarratea's webs: the wild scheme to crown Francisco de Paula, the salons, the bankers, the exiles. In this register the brotherhood is plain: in London the American lodges' old network of Miranda's heirs receives Belgrano as a brother, and around those guarded tables the future of the continent is argued in Spanish. He sits for the painter Carbonnier: the one portrait taken from life, mild-eyed, unarmored. Europe teaches him its lesson and he takes it home: the world wants monarchy tempered by law. Very well, then an Inca.

stops.name: Buenos Aires, el regreso del diplomático
stops.campa: Belgrano gives up the mission to Rivadavia's patience and sails home, reaching Buenos Aires as the summer of 1816 ends. He returns to a revolution unraveling: the year XV's anarchy barely survived, the north again threatened, the congress gathering at Tucumán to decide whether this is a nation or an episode. The government questions him on the state of Europe; his answer, given in reports and soon in person to the Congress, is a bell rung once: declare yourselves, for the world respects only those who exist.

stops.name: Casa de Tucumán, la sesión secreta del 6 de julio
stops.campa: Called before the Congress in secret session on 6 July 1816, Belgrano reports on Europe, republics out of fashion, thrones restored, and then lays on the table the most audacious proposal of his life: a tempered monarchy crowned with the dynasty of the Incas, the stolen house restored, the capital at Cuzco, America reconciled with its oldest blood. The deputies of the north acclaim it; the porteños smile at 'the king of the chocolates'. The plan dies in committee and lives forever in the canon: the general who wanted to crown the Andes.
stops.quote: Una monarquía temperada, llamando la dinastía de los incas, por la justicia que en sí envuelve la restitución de esta casa, tan inicuamente despojada del trono.
stops.quote_source: Acta de la sesión secreta del Congreso de Tucumán, 6 de julio de 1816

stops.name: San Miguel de Tucumán, el 9 de Julio
stops.campa: On 9 July 1816 the Congress declares the United Provinces a free and independent nation, breaking the last fiction of the mask of Fernando. Belgrano is in Tucumán and the canon sets him amid the days of celebration: the Te Deum, the illuminated streets, the dances where the general who made the flag sees it finally wedded to a declared nation. Six years he has fought under colors that legally did not exist for a country that legally did not exist; in one afternoon of winter sun, both are made true.
stops.quote: Mucho me falta para ser un verdadero padre de la patria; me contentaría con ser un buen hijo de ella.

stops.name: La Ciudadela de Tucumán, otra vez el Ejército del Norte
stops.campa: In August 1816 the nation hands him back his old cross: command of the Army of the North, encamped at the Ciudadela outside Tucumán. For three years he rebuilds it as what he always believed an army to be: a school. Chapel, classrooms, drill, gardens; officers examined in grammar as in gunnery. He holds the inner line while Güemes' gauchos, whom he supplies and blesses, fight the real frontier war in the passes. The sword rusts; the schoolmaster endures; the dropsy begins its slow siege of his body.

stops.name: Cruz Alta, el ejército arrastrado a la guerra civil
stops.campa: In 1819 the Directorio drags the Army of the North south, not against Spaniards but against the federalist litoral: brothers. Belgrano, swollen with dropsy, marches his army to the Córdoba frontier at Cruz Alta and no further: the armistice of San Lorenzo lets him halt a war he never wanted. He turns the army back toward Tucumán, gravely ill, writing that his one enemy is the enemy of America. The canon reads the halted march as his last service: the sword that would not cut inward.

stops.name: Tucumán, el motín y el general preso en su lecho
stops.campa: On 11 November 1819 Tucumán rises in revolt and the mutineers burst into the sickroom of the Army of the North's commander. The dying general is arrested in his bed: the man who gave the province its victory of 1812 held under guard by soldiers he taught to read. Tradition keeps the scene: Belgrano, bloated and grey, rising on an elbow to shame the officers with perfect courtesy, and the shackles falling away days later from pure embarrassment. He asks leave of a country in anarchy to go home and die.

stops.name: Camino de Santiago del Estero, el regreso del moribundo
stops.campa: In the summer of 1820 the general travels home to die: a jolting carriage on the endless flat road through Santiago del Estero, the doctor Redhead at his side, the provinces dissolving around them into the anarchy of the year XX. There is no escort worth the name and no government to send one; caudillos' patrols let the famous invalid pass. He is carried across the country he served like one more piece of its broken furniture, and he complains, the canon notes, of nothing but the patria's pain.

stops.name: Buenos Aires, el testamento en la casa paterna
stops.campa: In the house where he was born, on 25 May 1820, the Revolution's tenth anniversary kept by a city too convulsed to celebrate it, Belgrano dictates his will. There is almost nothing to leave: debts, back pay the state never rendered, a few books, the English watch. He commends his soul, orders the plainest of funerals, and settles his accounts with the exactness of the old Consulado secretary. The creator of the flag owns, at the end, less than a shopkeeper; the canon counts the poverty among his titles.

stops.name: Buenos Aires, la muerte y el atrio de Santo Domingo
stops.campa: At seven in the morning of 20 June 1820, while three governors dispute the wreckage of Buenos Aires in a single day of anarchy, Manuel Belgrano dies in the family house, aged fifty. He presses his gold watch into Dr. Redhead's hands, all he has left to give, and speaks his last words for the sick land itself: Ay, patria mía. One newspaper alone notes the death of the creator of the flag. They bury him in the atrium of Santo Domingo under a slab cut from a bedroom washstand's marble top, and from that poor stone the canon raises its purest altar.
stops.quote_source: Last words, 20 June 1820, as kept by the tradition and the testimony of those present
